title: 数据理解与阶段复测 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: Week 32 Listening: A Data Review Meeting

Mia: Hi, Tom. Thanks for coming in early. We need to go over the survey data before the team meeting at ten.
Tom: Sure, Mia. I printed the summary, but I noticed a few numbers look different from last month.
Mia: Right. The response rate was 68 percent this time, compared with 72 percent in March. That's a drop of four points.
Tom: Four points? That's not huge, but it's worth mentioning. Do you know why fewer people replied?
Mia: Possibly because we sent the survey on a Friday. Last time we sent it on a Tuesday.
Tom: That makes sense. Friday is a bad day for office workers. So, what about the satisfaction score?
Mia: The average score was 4.1 out of 5. In March it was 4.3. So it went down slightly.
Tom: Hmm. Still above four, which is good. But the drop is bigger than the response rate drop, isn't it?
Mia: Yes, the satisfaction fell by 0.2 points, while the response rate fell by 4 percentage points. They are different units, so we can't compare them directly.
Tom: Good point. I almost made that mistake in my notes. Let me correct that.
Mia: Also, the number of comments increased. We received 156 comments this time, compared with 120 last time. That's 36 more.
Tom: That's a lot of reading. Did you find any common themes?
Mia: Yes. The most frequent complaint was about the new booking system. About 40 percent of comments mentioned it.
Tom: Forty percent? That's nearly half. We should look into that.
Mia: Definitely. The second most common theme was staff friendliness, but those comments were mostly positive.
Tom: OK. So the main problem is the booking system. What about the age groups?
Mia: The 18 to 30 group had the lowest response rate, at 55 percent. The 31 to 50 group had the highest, at 78 percent.
Tom: That's interesting. Maybe younger people prefer shorter surveys.
Mia: Possibly. We could test a shorter version next time. Now, about the retest phase.
Tom: Right, the phase retest. When do we need to finish it?
Mia: The deadline is the 15th of next month. We need to collect at least 200 responses for the retest to be valid.
Tom: Two hundred. And how many do we have so far?
Mia: Only 85. So we need 115 more.
Tom: That's a big gap. We should send a reminder next week.
Mia: Agreed. Also, remember that the retest will use the same questions as the first survey, so we can compare the results directly.
Tom: Good. I'll update the tracking sheet and send it to you by Thursday.
Mia: Perfect. Let's meet again on Friday to check the progress.
Tom: Friday at two? 
Mia: Yes, Friday at two works for me. Thanks, Tom.

Section 2: Data, Decisions, and the Museum's Visitor Survey

Hello, everyone. My name is Sarah Chen, and I'm the visitor services manager at the Riverside Community Museum. Today I want to talk about how we use data from our visitor surveys to make better decisions. This is a simulated talk for educational purposes.

First, let me give you some background. We started collecting survey data three years ago. In the first year, we had about 1,200 responses. Last year, that number rose to 3,500. That's almost three times more than the first year. But more importantly, we changed the way we ask questions.

Originally, we asked visitors to rate their overall experience on a scale from one to five. The average was 4.2, which seemed good. However, when we looked at the comments, we noticed something interesting. Many people wrote that they loved the exhibitions but found the café too expensive. So we decided to ask more specific questions.

Now, we ask about different areas separately: exhibitions, café, shop, and facilities. This year, the exhibitions scored 4.5, the café 3.8, the shop 4.1, and the facilities 4.3. As you can see, the café is still the lowest, but it has improved from 3.5 last year. That's a significant change.

We also collect demographic information. For example, we ask about age groups. The largest group is people aged 35 to 54, making up 40 percent of visitors. Families with children under 12 are 25 percent. Students are 20 percent, and retirees are 15 percent. This helps us plan events. For instance, we now offer more family workshops on weekends because that group is growing.

Another thing we track is how people hear about us. Word of mouth is the most common, at 45 percent. Social media is 30 percent, and local newspapers are 15 percent. The remaining 10 percent comes from other sources. This tells us that we should invest more in social media, as it is growing fast.

One challenge is that not everyone answers all questions. Some people skip the demographic section. We have to be careful not to assume that the people who answer are the same as those who don't. For example, younger visitors might be less likely to fill in paper surveys, so we now offer an online version as well.

Finally, we use the data to set targets. Next year, we aim to increase overall satisfaction from 4.2 to 4.4. We also want to raise the café score to 4.0. And we plan to increase survey responses by 20 percent. These targets are ambitious but achievable if we work together.

Thank you for listening. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask.

Section 3: Data Interpretation and Stage Re-test

TUTOR: Good morning, both. Thanks for coming. Today we’re going to look at your data interpretation from the pilot study and then plan the stage re-test. Let’s start with the graphs you produced. Mia, can you talk us through the first chart?

MIA: Yes. This bar chart shows the number of students who completed the online module in three different weeks. Week one had the highest number—about 120 students. Week two dropped to 80, and week three was slightly lower, at 75. So the trend is downward after the first week.

TUTOR: Right. And what might explain that drop?

MIA: Possibly the deadline for another assignment. But I’m not sure—we didn’t collect data on that.

TUTOR: Good point. We must be careful not to infer causes without evidence. Now, Leo, your line graph shows something different, doesn’t it?

LEO: Yes. My graph tracks the average score on the weekly quiz. It went up from 60% in week one to 75% in week two, then fell to 65% in week three. So it’s not a steady increase.

TUTOR: Exactly. So the two graphs tell different stories. Mia’s shows participation falling, while Leo’s shows performance rising then falling. This is why we need to compare carefully. Now, let’s think about the re-test. When should we run it?

MIA: I think after week four, because by then students will have covered all the material.

LEO: But if we wait until week four, we might lose some participants. Maybe week three is better.

TUTOR: There’s a trade-off. A later test gives a fuller picture, but risks lower attendance. Let’s note both options. Now, about the sample size: Mia, how many students took part in the pilot?

MIA: Fifty? No, wait—it was sixty. I remember because we had three groups of twenty.

TUTOR: Correct, sixty. That’s a relatively small sample, so we shouldn’t generalise too much. Leo, what about the questionnaire response rate?

LEO: We sent it to all sixty, but only forty-five returned it. So the response rate was 75%.

TUTOR: Good. Now, for the re-test, we need to decide which questions to keep. Some items were too easy—almost everyone got them right. Others were too hard. We want a balanced test. Any suggestions?

MIA: We could remove the three easiest items and replace them with slightly harder ones.

LEO: Or we could keep them but add more challenging questions at the end.

TUTOR: Both are reasonable. Let’s aim for a test that takes about 30 minutes, no more. And remember to check the instructions carefully—last time some students misunderstood the scale. Okay, I think we have a plan. Let’s meet again next Tuesday to finalise the questions.

Section 4: Simulated Lecture: Understanding Data and Stage Re-testing

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about two connected ideas: how we understand data, and why we re-test at different stages. This is especially important for students who are learning to interpret numbers and graphs.

First, let's think about what data actually is. Data is not just numbers. It includes any information we collect—words, images, measurements, even sounds. When we analyse data, we look for patterns. But patterns can be misleading if we are not careful. For example, a graph might show that sales increased after a new advertisement. But that does not prove the advertisement caused the increase. Maybe the season changed, or maybe a competitor closed. So we must ask: what else could explain this pattern?

Now, let's move to stage re-testing. Why do we test at different stages? One reason is to check progress. If you learn something new, you need to see if you can still remember it a week later. This is called retention. A second reason is to find gaps. Maybe you understood the first part of a topic, but the second part is still unclear. Re-testing helps you identify those gaps.

There are different types of re-testing. One type is immediate re-testing, right after learning. Another is delayed re-testing, perhaps a week or a month later. Research suggests that delayed re-testing often leads to better long-term memory. But immediate re-testing can still be useful for feedback.

When you re-test, you should compare your results with your previous results. This is where data understanding comes in. You need to look at the numbers carefully. For instance, if your score went from 60 to 75, that is an improvement. But you should also consider the difficulty of the test. A harder test might give a lower score even if you have improved. So always ask: are these two tests comparable?

Another point is about sample size. If you only test a few people, the results might not be reliable. A larger sample gives more trustworthy data. But even with a large sample, you must check for bias. For example, if you only test students who volunteer, they might not represent all students.

Finally, let's think about how to present data clearly. Use simple graphs and avoid too many colours. Label your axes. And always explain what the data shows in plain language. Remember, the goal is understanding, not just collecting numbers.

To sum up, understanding data means asking critical questions about patterns and causes. Stage re-testing helps you track progress and find gaps. Combine the two, and you can make better decisions about your learning.

grammar.title: 比较结构、数量表达与指代综合；冠词和主谓一致检查
grammar.explanation: 本部分复习比较结构（如more than, fewer, the most）、数量表达（如a lot of, several, percent）以及指代（如it, they, this, that）的用法。同时检查冠词（a/an/the）和主谓一致（如The number of... is...）。
